title: Buy Virgin Atlantic Flying Club Points With 80% Bonus (1.1 Cents Each): Worth It?
summary: Virgin Atlantic Flying Club is offering a best-ever 80% bonus on purchased points, which works out to 1.09-1.39 cents each depending on where your account is registered.
content: Virgin Atlantic Flying Club is currently offering a best-ever promotion on purchased points. Through December 31, 2026, Flying Club members can purchase points with up to an 80% bonus, which is potentially an opportunity to buy points for under 1.1 cents each. Suffice it to say that this could be a very attractive deal. Link: Buy Virgin Atlantic Flying Club points with a bonus Promotion on purchased Virgin Atlantic Flying Club points Between 12AM GMT on November 24 and 11:59PM GMT on December 31, 2026, the Virgin Atlantic Flying Club program is offering a bonus on purchased points . Virgin Atlantic is offering a tiered bonus of up to 80%, as follows: Buy 1,000-4,000 points, get no bonus Buy 5,000-39,000 points, get a 20% bonus Buy 40,000-79,000 points, get a 50% bonus Buy 80,000-124,000 points, get a 70% bonus Buy 125,000-400,000 points, get an 80% bonus Note that the purchase of Virgin Atlantic points is non-refundable, and purchasing points doesn’t count toward Flying Club elite status. Points will be credited to accounts within 24 hours, though they typically post faster than that, and almost instantly. Buy Virgin points with an 80% bonus How much does it cost to buy Virgin Atlantic Flying Club points? The cost to purchase Virgin Atlantic points varies based on where your account is registered: If your account is registered in the United States, you’ll pay $25 per 1,000 points, pre-tax before any discounts or bonuses If your account is registered in the United Kingdom, you’ll pay £15 per 1,000 points, pre-tax before any discounts or bonuses On top of that, there’s a transaction fee of £15 or $22 The pricing is much better for those with accounts registered in the UK rather than the US. Assuming you’re eligible for an 80% bonus: Those with accounts in the US can purchase 720,000 Flying Club points for $10,022, which is a rate of $0.0139 per Flying Club point Those with accounts in the UK can purchase 720,000 Flying Club points for £6,015, which is a rate of £0.0084 per Flying Club point ($0.0109) Buy Virgin points for 1.39 cents each So as you can see, in the United States you can potentially pay 1.39 cents per point, while in the UK you can potentially pay 1.09 cents per point. It’s interesting how much Virgin Atlantic penalizes those in the United States when it comes to buying points. Then again, when it comes to overall points earning opportunities, we can’t really complain in the United States, given the amazing credit card offers we have . Virgin Atlantic is offering a bonus on purchased points How many Flying Club points can you purchase? Virgin Atlantic Flying Club ordinarily lets members purchase up to 200,000 points per account per calendar year, before any bonuses. However, during this promotion that cap has been doubled, to 400,000 points. Virgin Atlantic’s 787 Upper Class How does this compare to other Flying Club buy points promotions? When Virgin Atlantic Flying Club offers a promotion on purchased points, the best version of the offer is almost always for a 70% bonus. As you can tell, this offer is even better than those, as this is truly a best-ever offer. Personally, I’d recommend buying points based on when you have a short term use in mind, rather than based on the slight difference in the cost per point. Flying Club points purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as an airfare purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. Therefore I’d recommend using a card on which you’re trying to reach minimum spending , or otherwise, a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending . In addition to being able to redeem Flying Club points for travel on Virgin Atlantic, there’s also good value to be had for redemptions on Air New Zealand , All Nippon Airways , and Delta . Nowadays Virgin Atlantic has dynamic award pricing for its own flights, and for those with flexibility who want the best deal, this can make for some great deals. For example, there are some transatlantic one-way business class awards that cost under 30,000 points, which is amazing. Virgin Atlantic Flying Club points don’t expire . There’s no requirement to even have any account activity, as the points will never expire regardless. title: Why I’ll Never Fly Ryanair, Even If It’s The Only Option
summary: Remote airports, outdoor boarding and pricey daytime fares: here's why I vowed my 2023 flight would be my last on Ryanair, even when it's the only option.
content: Love them or hate them, low-cost airlines dominate the skies in some parts of the world. Nowhere is that more true than in Europe, home to Ryanair, the largest low-cost airline in the world (per 2025 passenger numbers). Back in my late teens and early 20s, I was all for booking the cheapest ticket to a place I’d never heard of, just because I could. That said, I still do still love to find a bargain, and can spend hours researching the best value option even when booking the simplest of itineraries. The buck stops, however, at Ryanair. My last flight was in 2023, and despite nothing glaringly awful happening, I vowed it would be the last. Airports are often in the middle of nowhere Part of the low-cost airline business model is choosing airports far from the cities they serve, since landing fees are often cheaper. One of the best examples of this is Frankfurt Hahn (HHN), located about 80 miles from Frankfurt am Main — the city the airport’s named after. After a quick check on the Uber app, a one-way Uber ride would likely cost around $180. A more wallet-friendly alternative would be this €24 bus. The journey time would likely be longer than the flight itself… It’s a no from me Even Ryanair’s largest base at London Stansted (STN) is around 40 miles from London, and requires a relatively expensive train or lengthy bus journey to the city. Ryanair makes passengers board outside, whatever the weather This is the part I hate the most about Ryanair. They are so stingy that they built their planes with built-in steps at the front boarding door so they don’t have to pay for air bridges. Whether it’s a sizzling 110+ degrees in the middle of the day in Seville, or deep in the minuses at Rovaniemi in Finland (the gateway to Lapland and Ryanair’s northernmost airport), you’ll have to brace the elements while boarding and deplaning. Admittedly, it wasn’t so awful boarding this 6 a.m. departure at Alicante (ALC) in Spain Reasonable flight times come at a premium Getting a deal on a flight departing at daft o’clock in the morning isn’t limited to just Ryanair or low-cost airlines. Who would ever want to set an alarm before 6 a.m.? However, Ryanair can charge such a premium to fly at a respectable time of day, that its fares end up almost the same as flag carriers. The screenshot below is a great example. British Airways’ one-way fares of 88 pounds from Heathrow (LHR) are over twice as much as two of Ryanair’s options from Stansted to Berlin. Low-cost airlines don’t always offer the best value However, Ryanair charges £74 for its midday departure (without a cabin bag). Compare that to BA’s 1:20 p.m. departure for £88 including a cabin bag; it’s a wonder why anyone would even consider Ryanair’s option if they needed to fly in the middle of the day. Bottom line Ultimately, airline preference is very subjective, and I know there are some die-hard Ryanair fans who won’t hear a bad word said about the airline. In its defense, if you’re heading somewhere off the beaten track, you can usually rely on Ryanair to get you as close as possible. Personally, I’d rather enjoy status benefits (and earn miles and status-earning points) by flying a legacy carrier like Air France-KLM, British Airways, or Lufthansa to the closest airport, then figure out ground transportation the rest of the way. Where do you stand on flying Ryanair?

title: Fascinating Air Saint-Pierre Domestic Transatlantic Flight Returns In 2027
summary: Air Saint-Pierre's once-weekly Paris to Saint Pierre and Miquelon flight is returning for summer 2027. Maybe this is the year I finally try it, even without a premium cabin.
content: One of the most interesting transatlantic flights will be returning yet again in 2027. Maybe this will be the year I finally get to try it, even if there’s no premium cabin angle! Air Saint-Pierre’s unique transatlantic Paris flights In the summer of 2018, an interesting domestic transatlantic route launched — it operated seasonally once weekly. Specifically, ASL Airlines operated a Boeing 737-700 that was marketed by Air Saint-Pierre between Paris (CDG) and Saint Pierre and Miquelon (FSP). A fascinating domestic transatlantic route What’s Saint Pierre and Miquelon ? It’s a self-governing territory of France, situated in the northwestern Atlantic Ocean, near Newfoundland and Labrador. The islands cover an area of about 93 square miles, and have a population of just about 6,000 people. The territory’s airline, Air Saint-Pierre, only has turboprops, which the carrier flies to places like Halifax (YHZ), Montreal (YUL), and St. John’s (YYT). Obviously these planes aren’t capable of operating across the Atlantic, so the airline leases a Boeing 737 for the once weekly flight. This was the first time ever that we saw a nonstop link between these territories and mainland France. There were some other things that made this route interesting: The runway in Saint Pierre is only 5,900 feet long, so the plane had to be weight restricted, meaning the flight could only transport at most 100 passengers (that means most passengers get an empty middle seat) I had intended to take this flight in 2018, but was shocked to find out that the flight was sold out on almost every single date that it operated; I wasn’t expecting that, especially given that the route was subsidized The route ended up returning in 2019, was then paused in 2020 and 2021 due to the pandemic, and then returned in 2022 through 2026. The route will now be returning yet again, for the 2027 season, so it sure seems like this is basically a permanent thing. Paris to Saint Pierre flights return in summer 2027 The once weekly flight between Saint Pierre and Miquelon and Paris will be returning in 2027 , between June 21 and September 6, 2027. The route will once again be operated by an ASL Airlines France Boeing 737-700, and the flight will be marketed and sold by Air Saint-Pierre. The flight will operate westbound on Mondays and eastbound on Tuesdays, as follows: Paris to Saint Pierre and Miquelon departing 4:00PM arriving 6:30PM Saint Pierre and Miquelon to Paris departing 10:30AM arriving 8:05PM The 2,664-mile flight is blocked at 6hr30min westbound and 5hr35min eastbound. As you can see, the plane sits on the ground in Saint Pierre for quite a while. This is so that the crew can get their rest and operate the flight back the next day, rather than making them stay there for over a week. I imagine the airline is able to get a decent deal on parking at the airport for 16 hours. 😉 It’s also interesting since this is an eastbound daytime transatlantic flight, which is fairly rare. Air Saint-Pierre fares to & from Paris for summer 2027 If you want to book a seat on this flight, below is the pricing for travel in both directions, with fares starting at €660 one-way for standard adult fares. Air Saint-Pierre fares from Paris to Saint-Pierre Air Saint-Pierre fares from Saint-Pierre to Paris As you can see, the fare difference just comes down to the age of the traveler, as well as the level of flexibility you’d like, with fares either being non-refundable and non-changeable, non-refundable but changeable for a fee, or refundable and changeable. The plane is in an all-economy configuration, as there’s no premium cabin. Air Saint-Pierre fare options to & from Paris Bottom line Air Saint-Pierre will be bringing back its flight between Saint Pierre and Paris in the summer of 2027, operated by ASL Airlines. This is an absolutely fascinating route, and it’s so cool to see that it was launched in the first place, and is sticking around. While the link between Paris and this French territory is obvious, it’s still kind of awesome that such a small territory can support a flight like this. But I guess the downside was fairly limited, since the route was subsidized from the beginning. Personally I find this to be the most intriguing transatlantic route. Anyone else love this Air Saint-Pierre flight as much as I do?

title: BermudAir Adding Flights All Over The Place: I Don’t Know What’s Going On
summary: BermudAir has announced a huge summer 2027 expansion, adding seasonal routes from Fredericton to Bermuda and from Nashville to Ocho Rios. The airline's strategy is increasingly hard to figure out.
content: BermudAir, the unusual boutique carrier that launched operations a few years back, keeps getting stranger. The company has just announced a massive expansion for the summer of 2027, and with this, we’ll see the airline add all kinds of seemingly random routes to and from Bermuda, plus all kinds of routes that don’t touch Bermuda. Whether you want to fly from Nashville to Ocho Rios, or from Fredericton to Bermuda, the airline now has you covered! BermudAir adds flights all over the place (don’t ask me!) For a little bit of background, in mid-2023 we saw the launch of BermudAir , a quirky niche airline with the goal of operating Embraer jets between Bermuda (BDA) and the United States and Canada. Initially the airline was going to operate all-business class planes, but it scrapped (“delayed”) that concept before launch , instead introducing a two-cabin concept (though business class just has blocked adjacent seats and better service). As I said from the beginning, the whole thing struck me as an odd venture, essentially trying to serve Bermuda year-round profitably, while going up against the major carriers that serve the airport. To my surprise, the airline is still in business over three years after launch, though it hasn’t necessarily been that smooth. As is pretty common for an airlines startup, the first years have been rocky, with several routes being cut after launch. For that matter, the airline faced a lawsuit over millions in unpaid airport fees at its hub, which isn’t exactly a great sign. Several months back, BermudAir announced new winter 2026-2027 seasonal flying to places other than Bermuda. Now the airline has announced summer seasonal flying for 2027, and it’s arguably even stranger. The routes are all over the place. In the summer of 2027, BermudAir will fly from Bermuda (BDA) to the following destinations: Burlington, Vermont (BTV) Fredericton, New Brunswick (YFC) New Haven, Connecticut (HVN) Portland, Maine (PWM) On top of that, the airline will be expanding beyond Bermuda, with new seasonal services in the following markets: Between Baltimore (BWI) and Guatemala City (GUA) and San Salvador (SAL) Between Fort Lauderdale (FLL) and Grand Cayman (GCM) Between Nashville (BNA) and Grand Cayman (GCM) and Ocho Rios (OCJ) Between New Orleans (MSY) and Grand Cayman (GCM), Ocho Rios (OCJ), Providenciales (PLS), and San Pedro Sula (SAP) Between Orlando Sanford (SFB) and Ocho Rios (OCJ) Between Raleigh Durham (RDU) and Ocho Rios (OCJ) Between San Antonio (SAT) and Belize (BZE) and Grand Cayman (GCM) Below is BermudAir’s updated map with destinations listed… BermudAir destinations in the summer of 2027 Guys, I really don’t know what’s going on here I really can’t make sense of what is going on at BermudAir. I feel like we’ve had reasons to be suspicious, when you look at the initial business model, vs. how things have played out: First BermudAir was going to be an all-business class airline, and then it backtracked at the last minute Then BermudAir was going to be all about Bermuda flying (I mean, with that name, you’d hope so, right?), and then it largely slashed that flying, as it increasingly looks at other markets BermudAir’s dispute with Bermuda Airport some time back over millions in unpaid airport fees certainly doesn’t built much confidence in the carrier’s sustainability I’m not suggesting there’s no demand in any of these new markets. The demand may very well be there. But there are a lot of challenges here: These routes are summer seasonal to the Caribbean and Central America, when that’s ordinarily the slow season for these markets, rather than the busy season, so this strikes me as counter seasonal flying It takes a lot of effort to build up demand over time, in terms of the local community actually being familiar with an airline and its routes, and that requires spending money on marketing and patience (which also requires money!) It’s especially hard to build up demand when you have less than daily service and fly to secondary airports (like Orlando Sanford), since the flight options often won’t show up in search results for the main airports It goes without saying that at this point the branding is just completely off; when you hear the name BermudAir, you don’t expect an airline flying from New Orleans to San Pedro Sula What’s interesting here is how the airline announced seems to be taking a similar strategy both for this winter and for next summer. So based on the fact that the airline is moving forward with its current winter schedule, maybe this is working? I don’t know… It’s also interesting how the airline actually got permission to operate these routes. As a reminder, Bermuda, Anguilla, and Turks & Caicos, are all British Overseas Territories, and Belize and Jamaica are former British Overseas Territory. How does the airline get permission to serve places like Honduras, though? I guess the airline is somehow getting permission to operate this as fifth freedom service, or something. BermudAir sure is expanding in an unusual way! Bottom line BermudAir is expanding rapidly, as the airline has announced new routes for the summer of 2027. Not only does this include several new routes to Bermuda (including out of Fredericton!), but the airline is also adding flying between the United States and Grand Cayman, Honduras, Jamaica, etc. I think BermudAir deserves an award for the most unusual route network of any “real” airline. I certainly can’t think of any other airline in this “league.” What do you make of BermudAir’s latest expansion?

title: Delta Plans Seattle To Singapore A350 Flights, Carrier’s Third Longest Route
summary: We know that Delta has huge growth aspirations across the Pacific, particularly to Asia. It’s an area where Delta has increasingly fallen behind United in recent years, but Delta now hopes to not only catch up, but even beat United. We’ll see what comes of that, and in particular, find out just how costly that growth is.
content: We know that Delta has huge growth aspirations across the Pacific, particularly to Asia. It’s an area where Delta has increasingly fallen behind United in recent years, but Delta now hopes to not only catch up, but even beat United. We’ll see what comes of that, and in particular, find out just how costly that growth is . A few months ago, Delta executives publicly confirmed plans to return to Singapore, a destination that hasn’t been served by the airline since 2019, when that was an intra-Asia tag flight from Japan. Executives also confirmed out of which airport the service would operate. There’s now an additional update, as an announcement about the new route is imminent, which almost certainly points to a fall 2027 launch for the service. Delta is eyeing Singapore for further Asia expansion As Delta executives view it, the airline is pretty maxed out in terms of its European potential, and in the long run, they see the most long haul growth potential in Asia, the Middle East, and Africa. So, what kind of expansion should we expect? So far, Delta has launched flights to Hong Kong (HKG) , and has announced plans to fly to Manila (MNL) and Tokyo Narita (NRT) ; Riyadh (RUH) flights were supposed to launch, but that has been postponed , and that’s technically Asia, but not a Pacific flight Delta also wants to connect its Los Angeles (LAX) and New York (JFK) hubs to Seoul Incheon (ICN), which is the hub of joint venture partner Korean Air, as Delta loves routing Asia traffic through there We’ve also known that Delta plans to once again fly to Singapore (SIN), and we’re learning more about what that will look like Delta is planning flights from Seattle to Singapore Back in August 2026, Delta Chief Commercial Officer Joe Esposito explicitly confirmed that the airline would return to Singapore. What was perhaps most interesting is that he also indirectly confirmed the hub out of which the service would operate — Esposito ruled out that the service could operate out of Los Angeles, so it’s pretty clear that the airline will operate this service out of Seattle (SEA). That’s also what JonNYC reported in the past, and now we can take that a step further — Delta is holding an event in Seattle in early December 2026, and that’s when the airline is expected to announce the service. Singapore as in. — JonNYC (@xJonNYC) November 23, 2026 My guess is that we’re looking at a fall 2027 service start, at best. At 8,070 miles, this will be Delta’s third longest flight, after its routes to South Africa, which are from Atlanta (ATL) to Cape Town (CPT) and Johannesburg (JNB). One certainly wonders if this Singapore route could be operated by Delta’s new Airbus A350-1000s , which will feature an all-new passenger experience . While the plane has great range and per seat economics, the only thing I’d say is that it’s “a lot of plane” for a new market, in terms of the overall capacity (even with the very premium layout). In both the Seattle and Los Angeles to Singapore market, Singapore Airlines is the only other carrier operating. So competitively there’s not a huge difference in that regard, though Los Angeles is a significantly larger market in terms of demand for Singapore, and for that matter, Singapore Airlines also has more service out of the airport. But perhaps Delta is also looking to beat Alaska to the punch in the Seattle market. Delta is hugely growing its presence in Asia My take on Delta’s Asia expansion plans It’s fantastic to see Delta looking to grow its presence in Asia. Point-to-point flying to Asia is a market that United has basically had cornered in recent years, and competition is good for consumers. It’s amazing to think for how many years Delta basically squandered its Asia advantage. Keep in mind that back in the day, Northwest had a robust Asia network, and after the merger with Delta, we saw that network decreased slowly but steadily, as Delta instead focused on routing everything through Seoul Incheon, and into the Korean Air network. So I’m happy to see a reversal of that strategy. I also have to say that given Delta’s hubris, it’s kind of fun to see the airline having to increasingly play “catch up,” rather than coming in as the dominant carrier. And I think that very much sums up what’s going on in Asia. The most basic structural disadvantage that Delta has is that United has a fortress hub in San Francisco (SFO), which is where a large part of its Asia network flies from. That’s fantastic for connectivity, not to mention San Francisco is a very strong market for Asia traffic. Delta, meanwhile, is taking a split hub approach, flying out of both Los Angeles and Seattle. Obviously Delta is trying to make the best of its situation, but there’s no denying that this is an uphill battle: Both Delta’s Los Angeles and Seattle hubs are roughly half the size of United’s San Francisco hub, so the connectivity and local loyalty just aren’t there in the same way Delta is in second place in Seattle, which isn’t great from a loyalty revenue perspective, given that Alaska continues to be the dominant carrier for the local community Los Angeles is a market that’s really hard to win, and if Delta can actually turn it into a profitable hub where it has a significant market share advantage, it’ll be the first airline to succeed at that in the long run Compared to United, Delta just doesn’t have the breadth or depth of network that United has; for example, one flight a day to Hong Kong is great, but United’s four flights per day are better It also has to be emphasized that in terms of actually transporting passengers profitably (or at less of a loss), United does a better job at that than Delta, despite its lower overall profitability. Comparing passenger revenue per air seat mile to cost per air seat mile, United is at 16.18 cents vs. 16.46 cents, while Delta is at 17.37 cents vs. 19.31 cents. Delta is trying to less reliant on Seoul Incheon & Korean Air Bottom line Delta is growing quite a bit in Asia at the moment. The airline has already launched flights to Hong Kong, with flights now on sale to Manila and Tokyo Narita. On top of that, Delta is expected to announce a new Seattle to Singapore route within the next two weeks, with a launch likely planned for the fall of 2027. It’s great for passengers to see more competition across the Pacific, as Delta sure is making up for a lack of effort for years. However, the airline will also have quite the disadvantage compared to United for a long time… What do you make of Delta’s plans to fly to Singapore?

title: Flydubai Resuming Israel Flights After Pilot Tried To Crash Plane Into Airport
summary: Israel's transportation minister has approved flydubai's return to Tel Aviv, pending security clearance, after a first officer tried to crash a 737 into Ben Gurion Airport.
content: On September 30, 2026, we saw an unbelievably horrifying attempted terror plot , whereby a flydubai Boeing 737 first officer attempted to hijack the plane he was second in command of, and crash it into Tel Aviv’s Ben Gurion Airport . He attempted to kill the captain of the flight using the axe in the cockpit, but thank goodness the captain managed to open the door after being struck, so that passengers could restrain the first officer. The details that have come out ever since have been downright chilling, including how the Omani pilot had specifically sought out a job at flydubai because the airline flew to Israel, and he wanted to crash into the airport there. Ever since that incident, flydubai has been banned from flying to Israel. For that matter, air service between Israel and the United Arab Emirates is just a tiny fraction of what it previously was. However, there’s now an update, and it looks like this service could resume very soon. Israeli authorities pave way for flydubai Tel Aviv return The Times of Israel reports that Israeli Transportation Minister Miri Regev has approved the resumption of flydubai flights to Israel, pending approval from Israel’s security authorities. This approval comes after a delegation of Israeli security and transportation officials traveled to Dubai to meet with their counterparts, to discuss new security measures to allow airlines to resume flights between Tel Aviv and Dubai. Emirati officials reportedly presented the Israeli officials with new steps that have been taken to ensure security in light of the incident, but details beyond that haven’t been made public. Per a statement from the Israeli Transportation Ministry: “The delegation today presented Regev with the steps the company has taken in the wake of the incident. As a result, Regev approved the return of flydubai, subject to clearance from security authorities. The move is a significant step toward restoring air connectivity between Israel and the UAE and expanding flight options for passengers.” Tel Aviv was flydubai’s single biggest destination, as the airline operated in the market with up to 10 daily flights. Previously, Israeli authorities had banned flydubai from returning to the country through at least December 15, 2026. Let's talk about that missing rudder of Flydubai 1073 B737 MAX 8. The aerodynamic forces involved may have been large enough to cause rudder failure through aerodynamic flutter during the extreme overspeed. The aircraft descended more than 14,000 ft in under 30 seconds. Even… pic.twitter.com/ECA34H4IXG — Turbine Traveller (@Turbinetraveler) September 30, 2026 Expect Israel to closely screen flydubai pilots Israel is typically known for its very tight security and good intelligence, but obviously there are lapses sometimes. One of the odd things about the flydubai attempted terror attack is that the Israeli government reportedly had a policy whereby pilots of foreign airlines couldn’t hold citizenship with countries that don’t have diplomatic relations with Israel. Oman and Israel don’t have diplomatic relations, so based on that, the first officer shouldn’t have been able to fly on the plane. However, it sure seems that there wasn’t actually enforcement of this rule, given that the flydubai first officer had flown to Tel Aviv several times before. I’d imagine that Israeli forces will now much more closely screen the pilots on these flights. I am curious if there were some new policies put in place beyond that, or if the extent of the enforcement here is that it’s about the potential nationality of pilots. Expect flydubai pilots to be closely scrutinized by Israel Bottom line Israeli authorities have met with their counterparts in the UAE, and the plan is for flydubai to be able to resume flights to Israel in the near future. This comes nearly two months after the awful terror plot, whereby a flydubai pilot intended to kill the captain, and then fly a 737 full of passengers into the terminal at Ben Gurion Airport. Some new security policies have reportedly been put into place, though the details of that aren’t being made public. I think one thing is for sure — Israeli authorities will carefully be scrutinizing manifests and keeping an eye on the pilots at the controls of these flights. This resumption is a big deal for flydubai, given that Tel Aviv was the carrier’s biggest market. What do you make of flydubai resuming Israel flights?

title: Island Mayor Pleads With Japan Airlines Mileage Runners After Locals Can’t Book Flights
summary: A Japan Airlines double Life Status Points promotion sent mileage runners to Okinawa's remote islands, booking up to 12 flights a day and leaving locals struggling to find seats.
content: The concept of mileage running is making headlines in Japan, and not in a good way. A lucrative promotion from Japan Airlines reportedly caused passengers to take up to 12 flights per day in remote markets, in some cases making it difficult for locals to book flights. What a story this is! Japan Airlines mileage runners book out island flights News On Japan has the story of how mileage running has caused issues for locals on some of Okinawa’s remote islands, as they’ve struggled to purchase Japan Airlines tickets due to a flood of mileage runners. While the story has been published in recent days, it seems to date back to February 2026 (best I can tell), when Japan Airlines’ Mileage Bank program was offering double Life Status Points for flights. This promotion incentivized all domestic flights equally, so some savvy frequent flyers decided to seek out the shortest flights, so that they could cram in as many flights in a day as possible. This ended up bringing them to Okinawa, where you’ll find some of the shortest flights in Japan Airlines’ system. These include flights between Ishigaki (ISG), Miyako (MMY), Naha (OKA), and Tarama (TRA). According to reports, some mileage runners booked up to a staggering 12 flights per day, leaving few empty seats on some essential flights. Japan Airlines mileage runners booked some short flights At Miyako Airport, some passengers were observed arriving with just small handbags, and then immediately heading to the departures area to board their next flight. As a few travelers explained: “It’s a route that lets me take 12 flights a day, the maximum possible. First, Naha to Miyako, then Miyako to Tarama. I come straight back, and after that I’m flying from Miyako to Ishigaki.” “It’s all the same airplane. I get back on the same plane, fly back, and repeat that 12 times.” “I’m taking eight flights. Once I get the status, my wife and I can enjoy the benefits together, so it’s worth it.” The issue is that this mileage running reportedly created serious difficulties for locals, who depend on the island flights for medical appointments, shopping, and other essential travel. There were some successive days in February where flights between Miyako and Tarama were booked out in advance, leaving locals unable to book seats. Here’s what some locals had to say: “Out of 50 seats, about 40 are taken by people doing mileage runs. What are we supposed to do? They don’t stay overnight here. They just get on the next flight and leave.” “I was planning to go to Naha for a medical checkup, but I couldn’t get a seat a week before. Everything was fully booked, so I couldn’t go.” “We have to take care of everything in Miyako.” Tarama Mayor Mitsuo Iranami even called on mileage runners to consider the impact their activities were having on the island community, commenting “I would like those doing mileage runs to understand the situation on remote islands and exercise some consideration, taking into account the number of people participating.” Japan Airlines reportedly even introduced measures intended to counteract this, including offering full refunds without cancellation fees, along with 500 bonus miles as an incentive. Below is a news story in Japanese about this, so you can watch that with subtitles, if you’d like. Loyalty programs are a powerful tool to fill flights! I think this story is a good reminder of just how well frequent flyer programs can work with the purpose of filling seats on planes… for better or worse! While it’s fairly common to see loyalty programs offer promotions, nowadays it’s rare to see deals that are actually that lucrative. When it does happen, we sometimes see that the people behind the promotion clearly didn’t think through all possible scenarios, and this is one of those situations. While Japan Airlines’ double status points promotion in February is pretty standard, the airline has added a new restriction for the offer this coming year, by capping the number of bonus points that can be earned during the promotion period, presumably to prevent something like this from happening. Obviously I feel bad for the locals in this situation, but it’s also hard to blame frequent flyers here for simply taking advantage of a promotion as advertised. Japan Airlines mileage runners booked out some local flights Bottom line Japan Airlines’ Mileage Bank frequent flyer program ran a promotion that might have just done too good of a job getting people to book flights, as a double Life Status Points offer caused some people to book up to a dozen flights per day, with some flights reportedly having up to 80% of passengers be mileage runners. Ordinarily that would be considered a success in terms of filling planes, but the issue here is that mileage runners descended on island routes that are also a lifeline for residents, given the efficiency of flying there. It’s not often you hear a mayor make a plea with mileage runners, but that’s exactly what happened here. What do you make of this Japan Airlines mileage run promotion situation?

title: New FAA Rule For Planes Lining Up On Runways May Cause Delays
summary: The FAA now requires a dedicated supervisor or controller-in-charge for "line up and wait" runway clearances, and one pilot already thinks that's going to cause delays.
content: The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has just added some new restrictions to how air traffic controllers can clear aircraft to “line up and wait” on the runway, in anticipation of takeoff clearance. This is intended to add an extra safety buffer, but to quote an airline pilot on an ATC frequency, “that’s probably going to cause some delays, that’s for sure.” New restrictions on planes holding on runway for takeoff As of today (November 24, 2026), the FAA has introduced a new rule regarding how aircraft can be cleared onto runways at airports. Air traffic controllers want to utilize runways as efficiently as possible for both takeoffs and landings, and that often involves having planes line up on the runway and wait, in anticipation of takeoff clearance. To give an example, sometimes a plane will be cleared for takeoff, and then a bit of separation is required until the next plane can depart. In those situations, it’s common for the air traffic controller to clear that next plane to “line up and wait.” The idea is that the plane then has clearance to enter the runway, and then await further takeoff clearance. After all, it might take 30 seconds or so for a plane to taxi from the hold short point of the runway, to getting into position on the runway. Under the new FAA rules, air traffic controllers will only be allowed to clear pilots to “line up and wait” in situations where there’s a dedicated supervisor or controller-in-charge who can’t perform other duties while these operations are underway. In the past this was a recommendation, but now this is a rule. Given constant air traffic control staffing shortages, this could actually impact operations a good percentage of the time. Here’s how the reason for this policy change is described: The core purpose of this change is to elevate the safety standard for Line Up and Wait (LUAW) operations by removing ambiguity in staffing requirements. By upgrading the guidance from “should” (a recommendation) to “must” (a mandatory requirement), the FAA ensures that the personnel providing watch supervision (OS/CIC) are fully dedicated to overseeing the safety of the operation without the distraction of simultaneously managing other operational tasks. The FAA is adding new rules for pilots lining up for takeoff How big of a deal is this runway policy change? I can appreciate the concept behind this, which is to improve safety. After all, we have air traffic controllers who are spread too thin, and all too often, they get a bit distracted due to the volume of things they have to deal with. That has definitely been a contributing factor to many accidents and incidents over the years. I do find the timing of this being introduced to be interesting, as it comes during one of the busiest travel periods of the year. I don’t think this will actually lead to any major issues, and for that matter, safety shouldn’t be compromised just because flights are busy. If you’re an observant passenger who is always looking out the window and is on Flightradar24, you may notice this policy in practice, for situations where you feel like the plane should already be lining up on the runway, but isn’t. I can’t imagine this policy change will lead to any major delays on a widespread basis, but then again, given how at capacity many airports are, even a little change can make a big difference. Below you can hear some talk between an air traffic controller at Albuquerque Airport (ABQ) and a Southwest pilot, where they’re discussing the change. As you can hear, the pilot says “that’s probably going to cause some delays, that’s for sure.” A new FAA runway safety requirement takes effect across the United States tomorrow, November 24, and an air traffic controller in Albuquerque is already warning pilots about possible delays. The change requires airports to have a dedicated supervisor on duty before controllers… pic.twitter.com/zxXariHNAy — Flightdrama (@flightdrama) November 23, 2026 While the FAA is making changes intended to improve safety, how about also requiring air traffic controllers in the United States to start using standard phraseology, like everywhere else in the world? 😉 Bottom line As of today, the FAA has added a new restriction on planes being able to line up on runways. A “line up and wait” procedure is pretty standard, but will now only be allowed in situations where the air traffic controller is only focused on one thing. Given how short staffed air traffic control often is, this could have some implications. I don’t think this will meaningfully slow things down on a national level, but for airports that make the most of every second to get planes in and out, it could definitely have implications. What do you make of the FAA’s new restrictions on takeoff?

title: Southwest Priority Card Review: Strong Airline Benefits For Frequent Flyers
summary: The Southwest Priority Card is my favorite personal Southwest card. Here's what its 90,000-point welcome bonus, $229 annual fee, seat perks, and free checked bag offer frequent flyers.
content: Southwest Airlines has several co-branded credit cards with Chase. Of the three personal cards, my favorite one is the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Priority Credit Card. This is my in-depth Southwest Priority Card review, covering the card’s benefits. I’ll also explain how despite this being the highest annual fee personal card in the portfolio, I still think it represents the best deal. Now is also a good time to consider applying for the card if you’re a fan of Southwest’s popular Companion Pass perk. Link: Learn more about the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Priority Credit Card Southwest Rapid Rewards Priority Card summary & key details for November 2026 Before I review the Southwest Priority Card benefits in detail, here’s a high-level look at everything you need to know about the card: Southwest Priority Card annual fee: $229 Southwest Priority Card welcome offer: Earn 90,000 bonus points after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first 3 months from account opening. Southwest Priority Card earning rates: Earn 4 points for every $1 you spend on Southwest Airlines purchases. Earn 2 points for every $1 you spend at gas stations and restaurants. Earn 1 point per $1 spent on all other purchases.. Southwest Priority Card foreign transaction fee: $0 Southwest Priority Card travel benefits with Southwest: Complimentary Preferred seat at booking, unlimited upgrades to extra legroom seats within 48 hours prior to departure, receive a first free checked bag, Group 5 boarding, 7,500 points every year on your cardmember anniversary, 25% back on inflight purchases Southwest Priority Card travel and purchase coverage: Auto rental coverage, baggage delay insurance, lost luggage reimbursement, travel accident insurance, extended warranty protection, purchase protection Best for: Those who fly Southwest several times a year and want seat selection benefits and the ability to earn points toward future award flights Here are my thoughts on the Southwest Priority Card’s main pros and cons: Southwest Priority Card pros Southwest Priority Card cons The most benefits among personal Southwest credit cards $229 annual fee Strong welcome bonus The points it earns are only useful for Southwest and partner awards 7,500 points every year on your cardmember anniversary Southwest Priority Card bonus, eligibility, & fees If you’re thinking about applying for the Southwest Priority Card , you’re probably most interested in the welcome bonus it’s currently offering, along with its annual fee and general eligibility rules for getting the card. So let’s dive into those. I’ll also explain a recent change to how Southwest cards factor into qualifying for the Companion Pass, which pertains to all cards, not just the Priority. Southwest Priority Card welcome bonus The Southwest Priority Card is offering a limited time welcome bonus : Earn 90,000 bonus points after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first 3 months from account opening. This is higher than the standard welcome offer for the card, and its minimum spending requirement should be easy for most spenders to meet. Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program , and based on my latest miles & points valuations , I consider Rapid Rewards points to be worth 1.2 cents each. So, to me, the points from this welcome offer are worth $1,080. Redeem Rapid Rewards points on any Southwest flight Southwest Priority Card bonus eligibility Chase and Southwest have some pretty strict rules when it comes to who is eligible for the card . The Southwest Priority Pass is not available to anyone who currently has a Southwest Rapid Rewards personal card, or anyone who has received a welcome bonus on a Southwest Rapid Rewards personal card in the past 24 months. However, you are eligible if you have a Southwest business credit card. This is in addition to Chase’s general application rules , including the 5/24 rule , whereby you typically won’t be approved for a Chase card if you’ve opened five or more new card accounts in the past 24 months. However, that’s not enforced consistently. When it comes to credit scores, there’s not a consistent score that you need to get approved for the card, though I’d hope to have a score in the “excellent” range. That being said, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been rejected, as it’s one of only many factors that determines card eligibility. Southwest Priority card annual fee & authorized user fee The Southwest Priority Card has a $229 annual fee. As a point of comparison, the other personal cards have annual fees of $99 and $149, so the annual fee on this card is a bit higher. However, as I’ll explain below, the benefits could justify the premium annual fee. The card also has no extra cost to add authorized users, so you can add those for $0 each, so that authorized user spending can help you rack up rewards. Southwest Priority Card no foreign transaction fees The Southwest Priority Card has no foreign transaction fees, so this could be a useful card for your spending abroad . This is a Visa as well, and Visas are accepted pretty widely around the globe. New Southwest Companion Pass qualification rules Another rule worth mentioning here involves how Southwest credit card welcome bonuses help you earn the Companion Pass , which lets you bring a companion with you on flights (both cash and award tickets) and pay just taxes and fees. For a long time now, the points earned as part of Southwest credit card welcome bonuses have counted towards the 135,000 qualifying points needed to earn the Companion Pass. But starting soon, credit card welcome bonuses will no longer count toward qualification. You’ll need to apply for a card by December 2, 2026, for your welcome bonus to count toward the Companion Pass for a final time. So apply for the Priority Card sooner rather than later if you’re hoping to earn that perk with the help of credit card spending. Now is also your last chance to get an annual boost of 10,000 Companion Pass qualifying points as a Southwest credit card holder. Starting next year, instead of a boost of 10,000 TQPs for having a Southwest card, you’ll get 10,000 TQPs if your TQP balance is 130,000 by December 31, 2027. That would be enough to get you to Platinum status, which will include unlimited Companion Pass trips as a benefit. This change eliminates the easiest way to earn this valuable benefit, and it’s not the only new rule: referral bonuses, anniversary points, bonus points from spending, and partner spending won’t count toward the Companion Pass either. In fact, Southwest’s rolling the Companion Pass into its highest elite tier, Platinum, and requiring either 140,000 TQPs or 100 qualifying flights to earn it. Southwest Priority Card rewards structure Beyond the Southwest Priority Card airline benefits, a major draw is the card’s points earning on every purchase you make — plus how it can help you work toward Southwest elite status through earning Tier Qualifying Points. Southwest Priority Card points earning The Southwest Priority Card offers the following points for credit card spending: 4x points on Southwest purchases — a 4.8% return based on my valuations 2x points at gas stations — a 2.4% return based on my valuations 2x points at restaurants — a 2.4% return based on my valuations 1x point on all other purchases — a 1.2% return based on my valuations Personally, I’d generally only put spending on the card if you’re going for A-List status and/or Companion Pass, because there are better cards for everyday spending otherwise. But still, those are some fairly solid bonus categories. Earn bonus points on Southwest purchases with the Priority Card Southwest Priority Card status earning As part of an overhaul of the Rapid Rewards program , Southwest is simplifying TQP earning on credit cards. Starting in 2027, every dollar spent on a co-branded Southwest credit card will earn you one TQP. In other words, $35K in spending would earn you Silver, $65K in spending would earn you Gold, and $140K in spending would earn you Platinum. This earning rate is the same across cards, so this isn’t specific to the Southwest Priority Card. Southwest Rapid Rewards elite requirements Southwest Priority Card points redemptions I have a dedicated post that covers how to redeem Southwest Rapid Rewards points for maximum value , but let’s briefly look at how you can use the points you earn from the Southwest Priority Card . Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, meaning that the value you get from your points is tied to the cash cost of Southwest tickets. There are a few different levels, ranging from Basic tickets to Choice Extra fares, so the exact value can vary a bit. Basic award fares tend to offer the best redemption value. You’ll also usually get the best value on international Southwest routes to destinations like Costa Rica and Aruba. I’ve been able to get about 2.0 cents per point on these redemptions. Starting in spring 2027, Southwest will add points earning and redemption opportunities with select airline partners, which should make your Rapid Rewards points more valuable for international travel. The planned partners include Icelandair, China Airlines, and Etihad Airways — I look forward to seeing how these add value to the program. The Southwest Priority Card could be worth it if you fly Southwest several times a year and value its seat selection and extra legroom upgrade benefits. The Southwest Priority Card is better than the Southwest Premier Card in terms of potential value and benefits, but its annual fee is $80 higher.
